analysis.one_liner: Requires every federal regulation to pass both chambers of Congress before taking effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees in January 2001 and sent to a subcommittee the next month, where it died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, an agency like the EPA or OSHA could write a rule, but the rule would have no legal force until a majority of the House and Senate passed a bill made of the rule's exact text and the President signed it. Agencies would send each rule to Congress, and Congress would have to act on it within 60 days under special fast-track rules. Since Congress passes only a handful of bills a year and thousands of rules are issued, in practice most regulations would simply die. The bill was pitched as making Congress accountable for the laws it delegates, but its real-world effect would be to shut down most federal rulemaking — including rules on air and water quality, workplace safety, food safety, and financial conduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries that federal regulations constrain. Any rule an industry disliked could be stopped simply by Congress never scheduling a vote, and the sheer volume of rulemaking guarantees most rules would never be enacted at all. Industries would face far fewer binding standards on pollution, product safety, labor conditions, and financial practices.

how_it_helps.text: Every new federal regulation would need an affirmative majority vote in both the House and Senate, plus the President's signature, before it could take effect [S2][S3].

The bill creates a fast-track path: the leadership of each chamber must introduce a bill containing the rule's exact text within three days, the bill cannot be amended, debate is capped at one hour, and a final vote must come within 60 calendar days [S3].

Rules exempted from this process are only the narrow ones — case-specific decisions, interpretive statements, policies, and internal agency procedures — so essentially all substantive rulemaking would need congressional approval [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal agencies to enforce standards. Air and water quality rules, workplace safety standards, food and drug safety rules, consumer financial protections, and environmental limits would all require individual acts of Congress. Congress cannot vote on thousands of rules a year, so most would expire unenacted — and any rule a well-connected interest opposed could be quietly killed by inaction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill's stated purpose is constitutional accountability: Congress currently delegates lawmaking to executive-branch agencies, and supporters argue unelected officials should not make binding law [S3]. That is a real structural objection to modern government, and the bill attempts to solve it by forcing votes.

The design is not workable at scale: agencies issue thousands of binding rules each year while the fast-track procedure still requires both chambers to pass each one separately within 60 days [S3]. Congress already struggles to fund the government on time, so the predictable result is that most rules — including ones the public strongly supports — would lapse by default, not by deliberate decision.

The fast-track design removes ordinary safeguards: the bill cannot be referred to committee, cannot be amended, points of order are waived, and debate is limited to one hour, so members would vote on dense technical rules with no opportunity to fix flawed ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine — Congress does write broad delegations and then avoids ownership of the rules made under them — but this remedy would break the regulatory system rather than discipline it. Requiring a separate act of Congress for each of the thousands of annual rules means most rules never happen, and the ones industries most oppose are precisely the ones easiest to kill by delay. A member of Congress could vote 'yes' on accountability while ensuring no inconvenient rule ever takes effect. The cost to everyday protections far outweighs the accountability gain.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House sent it to the Judiciary and Rules Committees on the day it was introduced, a subcommittee got it in February 2001, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. J. D. Hayworth (R-AZ) introduced the bill on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress, with 10 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Rules Committee, which handles House procedure — an acknowledgment that the bill's fast-track machinery required rules changes in both chambers [S5].

On February 12, 2001, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where bills routinely go to die; there is no record of a hearing, a markup, or any further action for the remaining two years of the Congress [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it, so it expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead, in the sense that the existing system of agency rules — clean air and water standards, workplace and food safety rules, financial protections — stayed in effect rather than being subjected to a process that would have let most of them lapse. Regulated industries, which would have gained a built-in way to kill new rules, lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday people who rely on federal rules

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent cosponsored it.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee, and never reported it back to the floor during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for consideration of its procedural provisions and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsorship on record is partisan — a Republican sponsor and 10 Republican cosponsors — but there were no votes, so the actual partisan split is unknown.

industries.note: If passed, the bill would have required an act of Congress for every new binding federal rule, a bar most rules would never clear. Industries facing environmental, safety, and financial regulation would have gained a default veto over new standards; the public would have borne the cost in weaker protections.

Agencies would lose the power to make rules binding on their own, turning them into advisory bodies whose work needs congressional approval. Their function of writing and enforcing public standards would be hollowed out.
